images.title: Paddling a painted forest
images.caption: Colourful bald cypress, Xuancheng, Anhui, China
images.desc: People paddle through flooded woodlands in Xuancheng, Anhui, where fall transforms bald cypress forests into a striking display of amber, copper and rust-coloured foliage. Unlike most conifers, bald cypress sheds its soft needles each fall after they turn reddish-brown. Native to North America, these trees thrive in wetlands, swamps and floodplains, often developing distinctive root "knees" that rise above the water. Some specimens have lived for more than 1,000 years. In late fall, the still water reflects the colourful canopy above, creating a remarkable landscape that highlights the bald cypress's natural connection to wetland environments.

images.title: Peace among the peaks
images.caption: Lake Braies, Dolomites, Italy
images.desc: Lake Braies sits almost 1,500 metres above sea level in the Dolomites of South Tyrol, northern Italy. Surrounded by forest and the dramatic peaks of the Fanes-Sennes-Braies Nature Park, the lake is known for its striking green and blue waters. A 3.5-kilometre trail circles the shore, while traditional wooden rowing boats offer another way to take in the scenery. The lake is also a starting point for several mountain walks, including the Dolomites' famous Alta Via 1.

images.copyright: Polar bear and cubs by Hudson Bay, Manitoba, Canada (© Danita Delimont/Adobe Stock)
images.title: A future written in ice
images.caption: Polar Bear Week
images.desc: November marks an important time for polar bears along the shores of Hudson Bay in Manitoba, where they gather and wait for sea ice to form before returning to hunt seals. This annual event is celebrated during Polar Bear Week, observed in early November. Polar bears are powerful swimmers and highly adapted to Arctic life, but shrinking sea ice is forcing many to spend more time on land, making it harder to find food. The mother and cubs seen in today's image represent generations of bears that have followed this seasonal cycle, highlighting both the beauty of the Arctic and the importance of protecting the habitat these iconic Canadian animals depend on.

images.title: Mist among the trees
images.caption: Black Forest, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
images.desc: The Black Forest in south-west Germany is known for its misty landscapes, forested hills, deep valleys, lakes and picturesque towns. Stretching about 160 kilometres, the region is home to Feldberg, its highest peak at 1,493 metres, and marks the source of both the Danube and Neckar rivers. Beyond its natural beauty, the Black Forest is rich in history and tradition. Forestry has shaped the region for centuries, while its renowned clockmaking heritage helped make the cuckoo clock famous around the world. Today, the area remains one of Germany's most distinctive destinations, blending cultural heritage with striking scenery.

images.copyright: St. Bartholomew's Cathedral in Frankfurt, Germany (© AlxeyPnferov/Getty Images)
images.title: Ghosts of empires past
images.caption: It's Halloween!
images.desc: Frankfurt, Germany, provides a fitting backdrop for Halloween with St. Bartholomew's Cathedral and its striking Gothic tower. Yet the holiday's origins are even more intriguing. Many Halloween traditions are linked to Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival marking the end of the harvest season and the start of winter. People believed the boundary between the living and the dead grew thin, prompting bonfires, offerings and disguises to ward off wandering spirits. Later, the Christian observances of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day helped shape Halloween as we know it today. St. Bartholomew's may set the scene, but Halloween brings the ghosts, legends and mystery.

images.copyright: Sandhill cranes, Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge, New Mexico, USA (© Terry St.Louis/Getty Images)
images.title: Time to fly high
images.caption: Sandhill cranes, New Mexico, USA
images.desc: Winter transforms Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge in New Mexico into a haven for wildlife. Established in 1939, the 57,331-acre sanctuary provides an important stopover for migrating waterfowl and supports wildlife year-round. Sandhill cranes, featured in today's image, arrive in late October and spend the winter here, roosting in shallow water at night and feeding in nearby fields at sunrise. The refuge is a key wintering ground for the Rocky Mountain population of sandhill cranes. Other seasonal visitors include snow geese, northern pintails, hawks and eagles, while mule deer, coyotes and other mammals inhabit its diverse habitats.

images.title: Where mist meets millennia
images.caption: Standing stones at Avebury in Wiltshire, England
images.desc: As morning mist drifts among the standing stones of Avebury in Wiltshire, England, the scene feels almost timeless. These ancient megaliths form part of one of the world's most remarkable prehistoric landscapes, centred on a vast Neolithic monument built around 4,500 years ago. Avebury contains the world's largest prehistoric stone circle, as well as a massive henge and stone avenues extending into the surrounding countryside. Together with nearby monuments such as Silbury Hill and West Kennet Avenue, it forms part of an extensive Neolithic complex that has fascinated generations of visitors, researchers and archaeologists.

images.title: Where history stands watch
images.caption: Kunětická hora Castle, Bohemia, Czechia
images.desc: What stories could these walls tell? Rising above eastern Bohemia in Czechia, Kunětická hora Castle has witnessed centuries of history. Dating to the late 14th century, the castle gradually evolved into an impressive fortress and noble residence. Its elevated position offered commanding views of the surrounding countryside and helped make it an important stronghold.
